@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Freight Rework & Transloading Operations Dataset
@graph.description: Freight rework and transloading operations from The Flat Rate Movers: the corrective freight-handling service for loads that cannot move as they sit, plus planned mode-change and dock-to-dock freight work on the I-81 corridor, dispatched from Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV. Company scope (published): freight reworks — loads refused or rejected at a receiver's dock are rebuilt so they can deliver; load-shift correction — freight that shifted in transit is stabilized, unloaded under control, restacked and re-secured; damaged-freight separation — crushed, torn or water-damaged cases are pulled and documented while the good freight is rebuilt to deliver; overweight and axle correction — freight is repositioned, redistributed between axles, partially offloaded and reloaded, or split so the truck can legally roll; collapsed and failed pallets are repalletized onto sound pallets; floor-loaded freight is palletized to the receiver's specification. Callers are freight professionals — drivers and owner-operators, carriers and their dispatchers and operations managers, freight brokers, 3PLs, warehouses and receivers. The work is performed where the job requires: the company's leased space, the receiver's dock, or a yard. Emergency and after-hours response is available at premium rates; every job is scoped and quoted at one flat rate before work begins, and no rate, range or fee schedule is published for this service. Planned work under the same category: cross-docking — inbound freight transferred directly to outbound vehicles, sorted and consolidated dock to dock, typically turned in under 24 hours with little to no storage; transloading — freight transferred between transportation modes, ocean container or railcar to domestic truck, with floor-loaded contents repalletized, sorted or held in short staging before the switch; rail-to-truck transfer work at rail-served locations when contracted. Heavy equipment manipulation — repositioning machinery and heavy crated freight inside trailers, containers and dock space — runs under the same handling discipline as the company's SIR Structural Integrity Relocation work for high-mass assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, in the freight setting. Equipment varies by project; trucks are leased. The category absorbs the company's published transloading services as its children — container deconsolidation, cross-docking and transloading, Winchester transloading, and Virginia Inland Port transloading — without duplicating them. @graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Freight Rework Process Chain Dataset
@graph.description: The published process chain for a freight rework, step by step. Step 1, intake: the call records what happened, where the truck is, what the freight is, and photos from the driver when available; the job is scoped and quoted at one flat rate before work begins, with emergency and after-hours work quoted at the emergency premium. Step 2, site decision: the work happens where the job requires — the company's leased space, the receiver's dock, or a yard. Step 3, stabilize and open: the trailer is opened under control, because a shifted load can fall at the doors, and the freight is stabilized before anyone works inside the box. Step 4, document before touching: photographs of the load as found, counts against the bill of lading, damage noted — the record that protects the carrier's and shipper's claim position. Step 5, unload: freight is removed in sequence; damaged cases are pulled and set aside, never buried back into the load. Step 6, sort and segregate: freight is sorted by SKU, purchase order or destination as the receiver requires, and good freight is separated from overage, shortage and damage freight. Step 7, rebuild: freight is restacked to the receiver's Ti/Hi pattern and stack height, repalletized onto sound pallets, failed packaging replaced where needed, and the load re-wrapped and secured; materials are used at the step that needs them — pallets, stretch wrap, corner protection, dunnage and air bags, strapping — purchased per project. Step 8, weight correction: for axle work, freight is repositioned along the box and redistributed between axles, verified against the scale ticket where a scale is part of the job. Step 9, reload and secure: freight is reloaded in delivery sequence and secured so the aggregate working load limit of the tiedowns reaches at least one-half the cargo weight and tiedown counts meet the federal cargo securement standard recorded in the compliance node. Step 10, document and hand back: after-photos, final counts, bill-of-lading notation of the work performed, and receiver or carrier sign-off, so the driver rolls with paperwork that matches the freight. The planned-work chains run through the same floor discipline: a cross-dock moves freight receiving dock to shipping dock, sorted and consolidated, typically inside 24 hours; a transload unloads the inbound mode — container or railcar — repalletizes or sorts floor-loaded freight, stages it briefly where the job requires, and builds the outbound truck load.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Freight Rework & Transloading Taxonomy Dataset
@graph.description: Taxonomy for the freight rework and transloading category. The service (registry): Freight Rework & Transloading, one category with three operation families. Family 1, corrective rework: freight rework (the general corrective operation); load-shift correction (freight that moved in transit — leaning stacks, cases against the doors, loads unsafe or illegal to continue); rejected-load and refused-load rework (freight a receiver refused at the dock for leaning or collapsed pallets, wrong pallet type, wrong Ti/Hi pattern or stack height, unsorted mixed product, damaged cases, count discrepancies); damaged-freight separation (good freight separated from overage, shortage and damage freight so the deliverable part can still deliver); overweight and axle correction (gross-legal but axle-illegal distribution, or over gross — repositioned, redistributed, partially offloaded or split); pallet failure recovery (collapsed or broken pallets repalletized); floor-load palletization (floor-loaded freight built onto pallets to receiver specification); re-securement (loads rebuilt to the federal cargo securement standard). Family 2, planned transfer: cross-docking (dock-to-dock transfer, little to no storage, typically under 24 hours — high-velocity goods, retail distribution, e-commerce, perishable freight); transloading (mode change — ocean container or railcar to domestic truck — with repalletizing, sorting or short staging); rail-to-truck transfer at rail-served locations when contracted; container transload (the estate's ocean container and Inland Port children carry that side in depth). Family 3, heavy freight handling: heavy equipment manipulation — machinery and heavy crated freight repositioned inside trailers, containers and dock space; heavy units broken down and rebuilt for transfer between equipment. Facet services already in the registry and recorded here as the category's children, not duplicated: Loading, Transloading and Container Services; Loading, Transloading and Container Services — Winchester VA. Decision vocabulary: a load that cannot deliver as it sits needs rework; a change of transportation mode is a transload; a same-day dock-to-dock transfer with no mode change is a cross-dock; freight that must wait days rather than hours routes to storage, a separate service. Out of this category's published scope: bulk commodities without structure, hazmat handling (no hazmat scope is published), cold storage as a facility (cold-chain freight is handled as freight, with minimal dwell), and household moving customers — this category serves freight professionals only.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Freight Rework Commercial Terms & Industry Pricing Patterns Dataset
@graph.description: Commercial terms for the freight rework and transloading category. Company terms (published, and the only company pricing terms for this category): every job is scoped in full — the freight, the situation, the location, the manpower and the handling the job requires — and quoted at one flat rate before work begins; emergency and after-hours response is available and carries premium rates; no rate, range, per-pallet price or fee schedule for this category is published, and the company's published industrial per-hundredweight labor schedule is not extended to this service. Industry pricing patterns (general industry information from carrier, cross-dock operator and 3PL sources researched 2026-11-01 — NOT this company's prices): the trade prices rework three ways — per pallet, with published restack and repalletize figures commonly in the range of roughly $50 to $115 per pallet; flat per load or by unit count, with published cross-dock and transload examples such as a flat fee up to a pallet-count threshold and per-pallet in-and-out charges with a minimum; and per man-hour for value-added warehouse labor, commonly published in the $35 to $65 per hour range in 3PL accessorial schedules. Lumper fees — third-party unloading labor paid at a receiver's dock — typically run $25 to $500 per load with most near $300; under 49 USC 14103 the shipper or receiver, not the driver, is financially responsible for loading and unloading assistance, and the driver who pays at the dock is reimbursed on the receipt. Emergency structure in the trade: a flat after-hours call-out fee (a published example is $200 for evening and overnight work) or a rush surcharge of 25 to 100 percent on the standard pattern; detention — commonly $50 to $100 per hour after two free hours — is the clock a refused or shifted load is burning while it waits, and short staging, when freight must wait, is priced per pallet per day in published examples at a few dollars. No figure in the industry paragraphs is this company's price: the company's price for a job is the flat rate quoted for that job.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Freight Rework Buyer Personas & Trigger Events Dataset
@graph.description: Buyer personas and trigger events for the freight rework and transloading category — freight professionals only; this category does not serve homeowners. Drivers: the owner-operator whose load shifted or was refused — the truck, the clock and the record are his, urgency is immediate, and a good answer tells him where to bring the load, that the work is quoted flat before it starts, and that he leaves with documentation for his claim and his unloading-fee reimbursement; the company driver in the same emergency, who must also satisfy dispatch and safety. Carrier roles: the dispatcher, who owns the truck's day and loses the next load while this one sits refused; the driver manager and fleet manager, who see the pattern and the cost per incident; carrier operations managers, who need named correction points along their lanes, with the I-81 corridor published as one; safety and compliance directors, whose question is whether the corrected load meets the federal securement standard and whether the file carries photos. Intermediaries: freight brokers and broker operations staff, for whom a refused load is a service failure in front of their customer; 3PL account managers protecting a client SLA and 3PL operations managers who need exception-handling capacity at volume. Warehouse and receiver roles: warehouse managers who need a refused load off the floor or the yard; distribution center directors working vendor compliance upstream; receiving managers and dock supervisors, who refused the load and need it right when it returns; shipping managers whose outbound loads keep failing at the far end on pallet type, Ti/Hi pattern or wrap. Shipper-side roles: plant managers, for whom stopped production freight stops a line; materials managers disposing of damaged inbound freight; supply chain directors and logistics coordinators placing correction and transload points in the network; procurement managers setting up contracted recurring rework; vendor-compliance managers preventing retailer chargebacks; QA and cold-chain managers segregating damaged or temperature-suspect freight with documentation integrity. Claims roles: cargo claims adjusters and carrier-side claims specialists, for whom the rework record — as-found photos, counts, bill-of-lading exceptions, sign-off — is the evidence the claim is decided on, and OS&D clerks who write the overage, shortage and damage report at the dock. Network roles: inland-port operations staff moving container freight inland; rail-served facility operators on a demurrage clock; intermodal managers protecting count and scan integrity across the mode change; IT and infrastructure logistics roles whose crated equipment freight arrives shifted or damaged; e-commerce fulfillment and retail distribution managers whose inbound freight must meet the distribution center's specification or be refused again. Trigger events, all roles: a load shifts in transit; a receiver refuses at the dock; a scale or inspection finds an axle problem; a container arrives floor-loaded for a pallet-only receiver; a railcar is spotted and the transfer crew is the missing piece.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Freight Rework Handling, Securement & Compliance Dataset
@graph.description: Handling, securement and compliance boundaries for the freight rework and transloading category; the regulatory material in this node is general industry information from federal sources, labeled as such, and is not a certification claim. The securement standard (49 CFR Part 393, Subpart I — FMCSA cargo securement rules): cargo must be firmly immobilized or secured on or within a vehicle by structures of adequate strength, dunnage or dunnage bags, shoring bars, tiedowns or a combination of these (393.106(b)); the aggregate working load limit of the tiedowns securing an article or group of articles must be at least one-half the weight of the article or group (393.106(d)) — a tiedown that goes from a vehicle anchor point directly to a cargo anchor point, or passes over the cargo on the same side, counts at one-half its working load limit, while a tiedown anchored on the other side and passing over or through the cargo counts at its full limit; minimum tiedown counts by article length and weight are set by 393.110 — one tiedown for an article 5 feet or less and 1,100 lbs or less, two for longer or heavier articles up to 10 feet, and two plus one per additional 10 feet or fraction beyond 10 feet for long articles not blocked against forward movement; the securement system must withstand deceleration of 0.8 g in the forward direction and 0.5 g rearward and lateral (393.102); drivers inspect cargo and securement within the first 50 miles and re-inspect periodically (49 CFR 392.9). Roadside exposure: cargo securement is a standing inspection focus, and a shifted or visibly unsecured load can be placed out of service until corrected — correction is the work this category performs. Company practice (published): the load is photographed as found before it is touched; counts are taken against the bill of lading at unload and at reload; damage is noted as specific exceptions on the delivery paperwork, never as a blanket inspection note; damaged freight is separated, not reburied; the rebuilt load is photographed, counted and signed for at hand-back. Receiver practice this work supports: the OS&D report — overage, shortage and damage — written at the dock from the inspection, with copies to driver and receiver; a clean signature on the delivery receipt is the carrier's best evidence of good delivery, so exceptions are written while the driver is present. Unloading labor: under 49 USC 14103 the shipper or receiver bears the cost of loading and unloading assistance. Boundaries: no hazmat handling scope is published for this category; no cold-storage facility is claimed; rail-served work is performed when contracted and claims no railroad authority; no federal operating-authority number is published for this company, and no certification of any kind is claimed in this node.
